1.pericope_label: The sons of the prophets build by Jordan, and Elisha raises the sunken axe head

schools.summary: Henry takes the college to be the one at Gilgal and supposes that wherever Elisha resided as many as could flocked to him, so that their wanting room is a good hearing, a sign many are added to them, his miracles doubtless having drawn them in. He reads their character out of the request: when they wanted room they did not speak of cedars and marble and curious artificers but only of getting every man a beam; they were poor men with no interest in great ones, too poor to hire workmen or buy tools and obliged to borrow, poverty being no bar to prophecy; and they were industrious, unwilling to live like idle drones upon the labours of others. On the lost axe he builds the man’s character, since he did not say it was a mischance and who could help it, but cried out with deep concern, for had the axe been his own it would only have grieved him that he could be no further serviceable to his brethren, whereas now it grieved him that he could not be just to the owner; and to those who have an honest mind the sorest grievance of poverty is being rendered unable to pay their just debts. Of the miracle he warns against doubling it, since we need not suppose the stick sank to fetch up the iron: it was enough as a signal of the divine summons to the iron to rise.

Ellicott corrects the rendering of the first verse, which is rather the place where we sit before thee, habitually, for instruction, so that the common hall is meant; and he adds that these disciples did not live in one building like a community of monks, their settlement being called dwellings in the plural, and that they could be married. He supplies the setting, that the Jordan valley was well wooded, its bed still overarched by oleanders, acacias and thorns, so that if all took part the work would soon be done. On the lament he notes that the subject is made prominent by being put first, implying that something happened to the iron. Of the miracle he is the most exact: the axe-head did not swim but simply rose to the surface, having fallen in near the bank, and the stick was a symbolical act meant to help the witnesses see that the rising was supernatural and wrought through the prophet, as the salt thrown into the spring at Jericho had been; it showed that iron could be made to float like wood by the sovereign power of Jehovah. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the word means borrowed at all, holding it means begged, and note that the exclamation implied a petition for help; and they dismiss the natural reading repeated by Thenius, that Elisha struck the eye of the axe with a long stick and so levered it up, as needing no refutation, since raising an iron axe that way and making it float is impossible.

Clarke observes that notwithstanding the general profligacy of Israel the schools of the prophets increased, which was no doubt owing to Elisha’s influence. He keeps the received sense of the lament and offers two ways of taking the clause, that the axe has fallen in and been sought in vain, or that it was borrowed and the loss the more afflicting, adding from Jarchi the words I have nothing wherewith to repay it. Of the miracle he insists the stick had no natural tendency to raise the iron and was only a sign the prophet chose to use, the floating being a real miracle, since the gravity of the metal must for ever have kept it at the bottom. Wesley gathers from the episode that although the sons of the prophets principally devoted themselves to religious exercises, they sometimes employed themselves about manual arts.

Gill glosses the sons of the prophets as their disciples, with the Targum, and adds that the place they went to lay some six miles from Gilgal. Of the prophet’s question where the axe fell he observes that though endowed with a spirit of prophecy he did not know all things at all times, and that if he did know he might have asked in order to lead on to the performance of the miracle.

positions.view: A bare sign with no natural tendency to raise the iron; the floating itself was the miracle, since the metal’s gravity must have kept it down
A symbolical act to make the witnesses see that the rising was supernatural and wrought through the prophet, like the salt cast into the spring at Jericho
Not a lever: the natural explanation repeated by Thenius is physically impossible and needs no refutation
Not a hook either: we need not suppose it sank to fetch up the iron, it being enough as a signal of the divine summons

debates.question: Was the axe borrowed or begged?

positions.view: Begged, not borrowed; and the exclamation was itself a petition for help
Borrowed, which is why the loss was the more afflicting — Jarchi adding that he had nothing wherewith to repay it

outliers.claim: Alone in correcting the picture of the school itself — a hall where disciples sat for instruction, not a monastic house, its members living in scattered dwellings and free to marry.
Alone in testing the rationalising explanation against physics, and in rendering the lost tool begged rather than borrowed.

themes: Behold now, the place where we dwell with thee is too strait for us
Let us go, we pray thee, unto Jordan, and take thence every man a beam
as one was felling a beam, the axe head fell into the water: and he cried, and said, Alas, master! for it was borrowed
And he cut down a stick, and cast it in thither; and the iron did swim

8.pericope_label: Elisha betrays the Syrian ambushes, and the king of Syria learns who is telling

schools.summary: Clarke admits the real or pretended cause of the war cannot be told, and borrows Calmet’s maxim that an ambitious and restless prince always finds a sufficiency of reasons to colour his enterprises; he supposes the Syrian had observed from the disposition of the Israelite army which way it was about to move and laid his ambuscades accordingly. Of the king of Israel’s response he reports that the Vulgate gives the verse a different turn, that he sent beforehand and took possession of the place so that the Syrians were disappointed, which Clarke thinks very likely although it is not expressed in the Hebrew. Wesley says simply that he sent soldiers to secure the place and passage designed.

Ellicott corrects the tense, since the king of Syria was warring continually rather than opening a war, and argues the reign intended cannot be a later one, since here the Syrians achieve nothing. On the plan itself he notes that the phrase for the place means a certain one, I will not mention which, and that the word for my camp occurs only here, its form anomalous and probably corrupt; the Targum renders house of my camp, while the Syriac and Vulgate make it an ambush, which has suggested that the true reading is hide ye, though he thinks it a more obvious change to read ye shall go down. At the next verse he defends the Authorised Version against those same versions, which deduced hiding from going down as though crouching on the ground were meant, whereas the word is really an irregular participial form from the verb to descend. He takes the king of Israel to have sent a sufficient force to hold the place, and reads the words not once nor twice as covering the whole verse. Of the Syrian king’s alarm he renders the term literally storm-tost, a phrase found nowhere else in the Old Testament, and reports that the question he put occurs only here, that pointed differently it would yield the Greek sense, who betrays me to the king of Israel, and that Boettcher’s correction, who leads us astray, is better still, being the natural supposition of a king unexpectedly confronting an armed Israelite force. Keil and Delitzsch defend the received text of the plan, holding the word for encamping quite appropriate, so that there is no need either for the alteration into ye shall hide yourselves or for Ewald’s ye shall place an ambush with its arbitrarily postulated meaning.

Gill alone makes the king’s compliance distrust: he sent spies to see whether the Syrians were there and whether the man of God had told him truth, for he had no hearty respect for the prophet though the prophet had been so serviceable to him. Of the Syrian king’s state he expands the figure Ellicott translates, that there was as it were a storm in his breast, and he was like a troubled sea, fretting at the disappointment time after time.

Henry sets the episode beside the last, since Elisha serves the king with his spirit of prophecy as he had served the sons of the prophets, whatever abilities a man has of doing good making him a debtor to the wise and the unwise alike. From the servant’s answer he draws the chapter’s theological point: a confession of the boundless knowledge of Israel’s God, as before of his boundless power, is here extorted from Syrians, since nothing done or said or thought by any person in any place is out of the reach of his cognizance.

debates.question: Is the Hebrew of the Syrian plan sound?

positions.view: Probably corrupt: the word for my camp occurs only here and is anomalous; better to read ye shall go down
Sound: the word for encamping is quite appropriate, and neither Thenius’s nor Ewald’s emendation is needed

debates.question: What did the king of Israel send to the place?

positions.view: Troops, to occupy it first, as the Vulgate implies — very likely, though not expressed in the Hebrew
A force sufficient to hold it, so that the Syrians returned unsuccessful
Soldiers, to secure the place and the passage designed
Spies, to test whether the prophet had told him the truth — for he had no hearty respect for him

outliers.claim: Alone in reading the king’s obedience as suspicion of the prophet rather than confidence in him.
Alone in tracking a single cluster of anomalous Hebrew forms through three verses, emending at one and defending the Authorised Version at the next.

themes: Then the king of Syria warred against Israel… In such and such a place shall be my camp
Beware that thou pass not such a place; for thither the Syrians are come down
And the king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God told him… not once nor twice
Will ye not shew me which of us is for the king of Israel?
Elisha, the prophet that is in Israel, telleth the king of Israel the words that thou speakest in thy bedchamber

13.pericope_label: Dothan: the host of fire, the Syrians dazed, led to Samaria, and sent home fed

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the scene, that Dothan lay on a hill twelve Roman miles from Samaria in a narrow pass on the caravan route to Egypt, and that the great host was infantry, not an army but a company, come by night to take the town by surprise. He observes that the servant was one waiting on the man of God, not Gehazi, who is never called Elisha’s minister, and that he had gone out to where the house commanded a view of the valley in which the Syrians lay. On the stroke that followed he notes that the word is the one used of the blinding at the door in Genesis and nowhere else, denoting not so much blindness as a dazing with mental bewilderment, so that they saw but knew not what. Of the prophet’s words to them he finds it easier to suppose the dazing had set them wandering in the valley, vainly seeking the way up to the city gate, so that a prophet finding them so spoke the literal truth. At the end he alone will allow no gratitude on the Syrian side: the stress lies on the word bands, for the Syrians, dreading Elisha, gave up clandestine raiding only to try regular war with their whole strength. Keil and Delitzsch say plainly that the prophet’s words contain a falsehood, to be judged as every ruse is by which an enemy is deceived; and they hold that Elisha forbade the killing because the king had not taken the Syrians prisoners in war, and because the object of the miracle, to show them whose prophet they dealt with, would have been frustrated by their deaths.

Henry supposes the king had heard how a captain and his fifty were baffled in the attempt on Elijah, and so sent an army, as if the fire from heaven that consumed fifty could not as easily consume fifty thousand. On the stroke he is the most precise of the three who describe it: not stone-blind, nor so as to be aware of it, for they could see the light, but their sight was so altered that they could not know the persons and places they had been acquainted with before. He agrees with Gill that the prophet did not lie, since if they would see him they must go to another city. Of the clemency he holds that the most glorious victory over an enemy is to turn him into a friend.

Clarke turns the vision into a question: where is heaven, is it not above, beneath and around us, and were our eyes open as the servant’s we should see the heavenly host in all directions, for the horses and chariots of fire were there before ever his eyes were opened. Of the stroke he glosses it as confounding their sight so that they might not know what they saw and might mistake one place for another. He calls the king’s eagerness to smite them dastardly, since men who in open battle lay down their arms are entitled to their lives, much more those whom providence has put into one’s hand. Wesley adds policy to piety, that the act was one of singular charity and of no less prudence, since the hearts of the Syrians might thereby be mollified toward Israel.
Gill holds that the prophet answered most truly, though ambiguously, since he had come out of the city and was going to Samaria.

debates.question: Did Elisha lie to the Syrians?

positions.view: Yes: his words contain a falsehood, to be judged as every ruse by which an enemy is deceived
No, if the dazing had set them wandering in the valley unable to find the way up — then a prophet finding them so spoke literal truth
No: he answered most truly, though ambiguously, having come out of the city and being on his way to Samaria
No: if they would see him they must indeed go to another city

debates.question: What effect had the clemency on the Syrians?

positions.view: None by way of gratitude: the stress is on bands, for they merely gave up raiding in favour of regular war
It mollified them: the act was prudent as well as charitable
It won them: the most glorious victory over an enemy is to turn him into a friend

outliers.claim: Alone in conceding that the prophet spoke a falsehood, and in defending it as a legitimate stratagem of war rather than explaining it away.
Alone in denying the Syrians any gratitude, reading the following siege as proof that the clemency changed their method and not their mind.

themes: Therefore sent he thither horses, and chariots, and a great host: and they came by night, and compassed the city about
Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them
the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha
Smite this people, I pray thee, with blindness
This is not the way, neither is this the city: follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom ye seek
set bread and water before them, that they may eat and drink, and go to their master

24.pericope_label: Ben-hadad besieges Samaria: the famine, the mothers, and the king’s oath against Elisha

schools.summary: Ellicott reckons the eighty shekels at about ten pounds, observes that ass’s flesh would not ordinarily be eaten at all and the head is the cheapest part, and brings two parallels: Plutarch, that in a famine among the Cadusians an ass’s head could hardly be got for sixty drachms, and Pliny, that when Hannibal besieged Casalinum a mouse sold for two hundred denarii. On the king’s reply to the woman he holds the received text right, allowing that the margin would be possible in another context, and reads the words as the irony of despair, reminding her of what she well knew, that corn and wine were long since exhausted. Of the hidden child he suggests that the mother hid him to save him. He explains the garment under the royal robes: sackcloth was the known garb of penitence, which Jehoram had secretly assumed to appease the wrath of Jehovah, and that a king should wear it was a portent in his subjects’ eyes. He supposes Elisha had urged unyielding resistance in the steadfast faith that Jehovah would help his own, and had yet brought no help in this hour of need. Of the closing words he calls Ewald’s correction certainly right, that the king and not the messenger is meant. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the curses of the law had here been literally fulfilled, which made the king rend his clothes, and note that the elders were gathered in the prophet’s house, probably for counsel and consolation, which shows what position he held.

Clarke reports that some take the king’s reply as an imprecation, may God save thee not. On the cannibalism he pleads for the mothers so far as he can, allowing that the children may have died of hunger and only then become food for their desperate parents, and reports Jarchi’s view that the hidden child was already dead, hidden so that one mother might eat him alone. Of the oath he leaves it open whether the king attributed the calamities to the prophet or thought he could remove them and would not; and of the closing words he cannot tell whether the prophet, the messenger or the king speaks them, suggesting the prophet answering the messenger from within. Wesley holds the second famine item to be no dung at all, the word being of doubtful signification and nowhere else used, but probably a sort of pease which in Arabic bears that name, a coarse food much used among the poorer Israelites.

Gill notes that Ben-hadad was not at all softened by the humane treatment his forces had met with, and finding he could do nothing by ambush mustered his whole host for open war. Of the king’s reply he notes the marginal rendering, and adds that Josephus understood it so, that being wroth the king cursed her in the name of God.

Henry weighs the tone of the reply rather than its grammar: some think it a quarrelling word and the language of his fretfulness, but it rather seems to be a quieting word, since till God help us I cannot help thee. On the sackcloth he grants the grief and denies the repentance, since the king lamented the calamity but not his own iniquity, nor that of his people, which was the procuring cause of it, so that the foolishness of man perverted his way and then his heart fretted against the Lord. Of the oath he marks what it replaced: instead of vowing to pull down the calves at Dan and Beth-el, he swore the death of Elisha, as under the persecuting emperors the fault was laid on the Christians whenever the empire groaned.

debates.question: Is the king’s reply to the woman a prayer or a curse?

positions.view: Some read it as an imprecation, may God save thee not
The margin gives let not the Lord save thee, and Josephus took it so, that being wroth he cursed her in God’s name
The received text is right: it is the irony of despair, reminding her that corn and wine are long since gone
Not a quarrelling word but a quieting one: till God help us I cannot help thee

debates.question: Who says that this evil is of the Lord?

positions.view: It cannot be told whether the prophet, the messenger or the king — perhaps the prophet answering the messenger from within
The king: Ewald’s correction of messenger to king is certainly right

outliers.claim: Alone in pricing the famine against two classical sieges, and alone in reading the sackcloth as a secret act of appeasement that became a portent once seen.
Alone in naming what the oath stood in the place of — the calves at Dan and Beth-el that were never pulled down.

themes: Benhadad king of Syria gathered all his host, and went up, and besieged Samaria
an ass’s head was sold for fourscore pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver
If the Lord do not help thee, whence shall I help thee? out of the barnfloor, or out of the winepress?
